name: Random Forest pixel classifier for water, vegetation and built-up

identity.method_name: Random Forest (Breiman 2001) multi-class pixel classifier for water / vegetation / built-up land cover
identity.core_idea: An ensemble of decorrelated decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample of pixels and a random subset of spectral/index features at each split, votes on a class label per pixel. Applied here it would replace the fixed MNDWI>0 / NDVI>0.30 hard thresholds with a learned decision boundary over the five cached Sentinel-2 bands (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11) plus derived indices (MNDWI, NDVI, NDBI), classifying every pixel in each scene into water, vegetation, or built-up. It is the standard classical baseline for pixel-wise land cover mapping and is the correct comparison point for anything on the image side, not the 42-row table side.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. No official dataset ID applies; this is a bespoke classifier trained on the project's own cached Sentinel-2 L2A bands (Earth Search STAC, tile MGRS-43PGQ) and the OpenStreetMap lake polygon, using scikit-learn's RandomForestClassifier (not a named dataset).

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Threshold rule bootstrapped into weak supervision, with a real circularity risk. There is no ground truth for any pixel in this project, so training labels must be manufactured. Three realistic sources exist: (1) spectral-index seed labels -- take pixels far into the tails of MNDWI and NDVI (e.g. MNDWI > 0.3 as confident water, MNDWI < -0.3 and NDVI > 0.5 as confident vegetation, NDBI-positive dry pixels as confident built-up) as pseudo-labels, following the automated-training-data approach of Lasko et al. 2021 (Remote Sensing 13(22):4531, doi 10.3390/rs13224531), which was built for exactly this water-extent-without-ground-truth problem at 10/20 m Sentinel-2 resolution; (2) the Sentinel-2 L2A Scene Classification Layer (SCL) band, which ships with every scene already cached and gives a coarse water/vegetation/not-vegetated/built-up-adjacent flag per pixel from an independent Sen2Cor algorithm, so it is a genuinely separate (if noisy) label source, not derived from the project's own thresholds; (3) manual region-of-interest (ROI) digitising, where the student hand-draws a few dozen polygons per class per scene in QGIS using true-colour and false-colour composites as visual guides. Cost: (1) is free but risks circularity (see below); (2) is free and independent but coarse (SCL is not designed as a precise land-cover product, and its water/vegetation classes are cloud-masking byproducts, not curated targets); (3) costs roughly 0.5-1 student-day per scene-year to digitise a workable set of ROIs across 6 lakes, so 3-6 days total for all 7 years if done properly, or less if one representative scene per lake is used as a training scene and the rest are only predicted on.
fit_to_project.input_required: The five cached Sentinel-2 bands (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11) plus SCL, already available on the project's 20 m EPSG:32643 grid, from which MNDWI/NDVI/NDBI are computed as additional features; and per-pixel training labels, which are NOT already available and must be produced by one of the three strategies above.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: not-applicable-as-stated, but yes-if-reframed. This is explicitly a per-pixel method, not a per-lake-year method. A single Sentinel-2 scene over the study area contributes on the order of 900,000 pixels (per project_constraints.pixels_per_scene); even restricting to pixels inside or near the 6 lake polygons across 7 years yields many tens of thousands of labelled and unlabelled pixels. Sample size is genuinely not the constraint here -- the note is correct that label quality, not label quantity, is the bottleneck. However, the effective INDEPENDENT sample size for validation is still bounded by the number of distinct lakes and dates (spatially adjacent pixels within one lake on one date are highly autocorrelated, so 900,000 pixels are not 900,000 independent draws).
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels. No variant of this classifier can be trained with zero labels; it always needs either spectral-index seeds, SCL, or manual ROIs as described above.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Yes, this is a native fit. The classifier operates directly on the project's existing 20 m EPSG:32643 grid with no foreign pretrained resolution assumption; Lasko et al. 2021 explicitly validate an equivalent method at 20 m Sentinel-2 resolution (9-band VIS/NIR/SWIR ensemble), which is the closest published precedent to this exact setup.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: Spectral-index seed labels (from the project's own MNDWI/NDVI/NDBI), and/or the Sentinel-2 SCL band, and/or a modest manually-digitised ROI set. Not 'none' -- some form of weak or seed labelling is unavoidable.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Partially fixes limitation (1): by operating per-pixel rather than per-lake-year it sidesteps the 42-row ceiling for the image-classification task, though it does not add rows to the tabular model used elsewhere in the project. It does not fix limitation (2) (OSM buildings still a single snapshot; this method classifies pixels, it does not create a new time-varying building feature). It does not fix limitation (3) (no ground truth remains the core problem, only reframed as label-quality risk). It does not fix limitation (4) (still one dry-season scene per year, since the classifier is applied per available scene, not to additional imagery).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No better than the current MNDWI threshold unless explicitly engineered to. A drained lakebed during desilting is spectrally bare soil/mud, which a Random Forest given only spectral bands and indices will most likely assign to a bare-ground or built-up-adjacent class rather than water -- exactly the same failure the current fixed threshold already has (Bellandur 15.7 ha -> 0.4 ha -> 107.9 ha would still read as dramatic water loss then gain, indistinguishable from encroachment-then-reversal, unless a fourth 'bare/exposed lakebed' class is added and trained with its own seed labels). Adding that class is possible and cheap, but nothing in the RF architecture does this automatically.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Not automatically, and this is the classifier's most serious failure mode for this project specifically. Water hyacinth spectrally resembles healthy vegetation (high NDVI, low MNDWI), so a 3-class water/vegetation/built-up Random Forest will place hyacinth mats in the vegetation class exactly as the current NDVI>0.30 rule already does -- Bellandur's 2019 260 ha of vegetation inside a 315 ha footprint would be classified the same way. If seed labels are drawn from the project's own NDVI threshold, this is not an improvement, it is the same rule wearing a machine-learning label. A genuine fix requires a fourth class (open water vs. floating macrophyte) trained against the published Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843) as an external, non-circular label source -- this is feasible and is the single most valuable use of that paper in the project, but it is extra work beyond a default 3-class RF.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. The classifier's per-pixel outputs are aggregated inside the OpenStreetMap lake polygon, which per project_constraints.lake_boundary is not a legal boundary. Whatever buffer distance is tested downstream (30 m reinstated Master Plan buffer or the quashed 75 m NGT buffer) is applied to this same non-statutory polygon; the classifier itself has no mechanism to connect its water/vegetation/built-up map to Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority records, Survey of India records, Bhuvan, or the National Wetland Atlas 2024. It is exactly as legally traceable as the current classical baseline it replaces -- no better, no worse.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Every input feature (the five spectral bands and their derived indices) is recomputed fresh from each year's own Sentinel-2 scene, so all inputs genuinely vary year to year -- unlike the OSM building counts. However, per project_constraints.imagery only one scene per year (the dry-season minimum) is used, so the classifier sees 7 independent snapshots, not a real intra-annual trajectory; it cannot detect within-year hyacinth bloom timing or short desilting windows that fall between annual captures.

implementation.libraries: scikit-learn (RandomForestClassifier), rasterio/rioxarray for band I/O and index computation, geopandas for ROI polygons, numpy/pandas for feature stacking. Optionally imbalanced-learn if class weighting is needed for the built-up class, which will be spatially rare inside a lake buffer.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable. Random Forest is trained from scratch on the project's own pixels every time; there are no pretrained RF weights to import, and none of the label sources (spectral seeds, SCL, manual ROIs) require any external model.
implementation.licence: Fully open. scikit-learn is BSD-licensed; Sentinel-2 L2A data (including SCL) is free and open under the Copernicus data licence; OpenStreetMap building/lake data is under the Open Database Licence (attribution required). No licence blocker for an academic project.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial. Random Forest on tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand pixels with 5-8 features trains in seconds to low minutes on a laptop CPU; no GPU is needed at any point. This is one of the cheapest items on the entire list computationally, and is fully reproducible end to end by a solo student with no lab cluster.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 4-7 student-days total: feature engineering (bands + indices) 0.5 day; label generation, the real cost -- spectral-seed labels are near-free (0.5 day to script and sanity-check), SCL-based labels are similarly cheap, but a credible manual ROI set across 6 lakes and a handful of representative years realistically takes 2-4 days including cross-checking against the macrophyte paper for hyacinth pixels; model training and tuning 0.5-1 day; validation design (spatial hold-out by lake, see evaluation) and write-up 1 day.

evaluation.metrics: Per-class precision, recall and F1 (especially for the vegetation-vs-hyacinth and water-vs-bare-lakebed distinctions), plus a confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa. Overall pixel accuracy alone is misleading because water pixels are a small minority of the total scene (the 6 lakes occupy a small fraction of the ~900,000-pixel scene), so a classifier that predicts 'not-water' everywhere would still score high raw accuracy.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Spatial block hold-out by lake is the correct protocol: train the classifier on pixels from 5 of the 6 lakes (plus, if used, manually labelled ROIs from those lakes) and test on the pixels of the 6th, held-out lake, rotating through all 6 (a leave-one-lake-out spatial cross-validation). A naive random pixel-level train/test split is invalid here because neighbouring pixels within the same lake and scene are strongly spatially autocorrelated (adjacent pixels are almost always the same class), so random splitting leaks lake-specific spectral signatures between train and test and inflates the reported score.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Three concrete leakage paths: (1) spatial autocorrelation -- pixels a few metres apart within the same lake polygon are not independent draws, so any non-lake-based split overstates performance; (2) label circularity -- if training labels are seeded from the same MNDWI/NDVI thresholds the project's current method already uses, then a report that 'the Random Forest classifier agrees with / outperforms the MNDWI threshold' is close to tautological, since the classifier was taught to reproduce that threshold's decision boundary rather than an independent truth; (3) same-lake-different-year leakage, if pixels from the same physical location in different years end up in both train and test, the model can memorise a lake's specific shoreline shape and typical spectral signature rather than learning a transferable, generalisable rule.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None by default. A plain Random Forest outputs a bare class label (or a vote-share pseudo-probability) per pixel with no calibrated interval. Given that labels themselves are proxy/noisy rather than true ground truth, per-pixel class probabilities should at minimum be reported alongside out-of-bag error estimates, and ideally wrapped in a conformal-prediction layer (item C7 in this project's outline) before any aggregate 'X hectares reclassified' figure is presented to a panel.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable in the direct sense -- this is a per-pixel classifier operating on real, unaugmented spectral measurements, not a small tabular dataset needing synthetic row generation. The closest analogous risk is class-imbalance correction (e.g. oversampling built-up pixels, which are rare inside a lake buffer) via SMOTE in feature space; if used, this should be disclosed, since synthetic built-up pixels interpolated between a small number of real examples could smooth over the genuinely ambiguous cases (partially-built plots, bare lakebed under construction) that most need honest, non-fabricated treatment.

evidence.published_performance: Lasko et al. 2021 (Remote Sensing 13(22):4531, doi 10.3390/rs13224531) report an automated spectral-index-seeded training approach for Sentinel-2 surface water mapping at 10 m and 20 m achieving high agreement with reference water masks using ensembles of spectral-index thresholds combined with machine-learning classifiers, without manual ground-truth collection [verify -- exact F1/kappa figures were not independently re-derived here and should be checked directly in the paper before being quoted as this project's expected performance]. General Random Forest vs SVM vs k-NN comparisons for Sentinel-2 land cover (e.g. the PMC5796274 comparison study) commonly report overall accuracies in the 85-95% range for well-separated classes like water/vegetation/built-up when good training data exists [verify], but these figures are not transferable to this project because label quality here is the open problem, not the classifier choice.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Lasko et al. 2021 validate their method across multiple U.S. and international water bodies at Sentinel-2 10-20 m scale, not on Bengaluru or Indian urban lakes, and not on lakes carrying a hyacinth confound of the kind documented for Bellandur/Varthur. Generic RF-vs-SVM comparison studies are typically conducted over much larger, more spectrally homogeneous regions than 6 individual small-to-medium urban lakes.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No direct application of this exact spectral-seeded Random Forest approach to Bengaluru or Indian urban lakes was found. The closest domestically relevant published work is the Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843), which addresses the hyacinth confound directly for these same two lakes and should be treated as the primary Bengaluru-specific evidence source for this item, though it is a mapping study, not a Random-Forest-classifier study per se.
evidence.evidence_recency: 2021 for the closest directly relevant method (Lasko et al., automated training data from spectral indices at 20 m); 2020 for the Bengaluru-specific macrophyte cross-check. Both are within the post-2020 preference stated in the research brief; the underlying spectral indices (MNDWI, Xu 2006; NDVI, older) are foundational and remain in range per the brief's own carve-out.
evidence.primary_sources: Lasko, Maloney, Becker, Griffin, Lyon, Griffin (2021), 'Automated Training Data Generation from Spectral Indexes for Mapping Surface Water Extent with Sentinel-2 Satellite Imagery at 10 m and 20 m Resolutions', Remote Sensing 13(22):4531, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs13224531 ; Sentinel-2 L2A Scene Classification Layer documentation, ESA Sentinel-2 User Guide, https://sentiwiki.copernicus.eu/web/s2-processing (Sen2Cor SCL algorithm) [verify exact current URL]; scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier documentation, https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier.html ; Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte mapping, doi 10.3390/rs12223843; Xu, H. (2006), 'Modification of normalised difference water index (NDWI) to enhance open water features in remotely sensed imagery', International Journal of Remote Sensing 27(14):3025-3033 (the project's own current-method citation).

risk.failure_modes: (1) Label circularity: if seed labels come only from the project's own MNDWI/NDVI thresholds, the 'classifier' is a smoothed re-statement of the rule it is meant to replace, and any claimed improvement is not defensible. (2) Hyacinth misclassification: without a dedicated fourth class trained against an independent source, hyacinth continues to be counted as vegetation, reproducing the existing Bellandur/Varthur confound exactly. (3) Bare-lakebed misclassification during desilting: without a dedicated class, drained lakebeds will most likely be pulled toward the built-up or bare-ground class, manufacturing an apparent 'encroachment' signal that is really maintenance. (4) SCL as a label source is coarse and was designed for cloud/quality masking, not precise thematic classification, so labels drawn from it inherit its own systematic errors (e.g., known confusion of dark water with cloud shadow, and bright bare soil with built-up).
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask exactly the question the note anticipates: 'where did the training labels come from, and if they came from your own threshold, how is this not the same method wearing a different name?' The only fully defensible answer combines an independent, non-circular label source (SCL for a coarse cross-check, and/or a modest manually-digitised ROI set checked against the published macrophyte map) with an explicit statement that spectral-index-seeded labels alone would be circular and were therefore not used as the sole source. If manual ROIs are used, the panel will also ask about inter-annotator reliability if only one student did all the labelling -- a second labelling pass or explicit acknowledgement of single-annotator subjectivity is the honest mitigation.
risk.honest_expectation: As the genuine classical baseline for the IMAGE side, this method will likely produce a per-pixel water/vegetation/built-up map that is somewhat more nuanced than the current fixed MNDWI/NDVI thresholds (e.g., better separation of shadow from water, or partial handling of mixed pixels via probability scores), but it will NOT resolve either confound (desilting or hyacinth) unless a 4th/5th class and an independent label source are deliberately engineered in, and it will not, by itself, produce a defensible 'encroachment' number -- it produces a better land-cover map, which is a necessary but not sufficient step toward an encroachment claim. A modest, disclosed improvement over the fixed threshold is the realistic outcome; a large jump in reported accuracy should be treated as a red flag for label leakage rather than a genuine gain.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt -- this is the correct, cheap, and honest classical baseline for the pixel/image side of the project, provided the label source is genuinely independent (SCL and/or manual ROIs, not solely the project's own MNDWI/NDVI thresholds) and a dedicated hyacinth/bare-lakebed class is added rather than assumed away.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We used a Random Forest pixel classifier as the classical image-side baseline, trained on labels from the Sentinel-2 Scene Classification Layer and a small manually-digitised ROI set (not from our own MNDWI/NDVI thresholds, to avoid circularity), evaluated with leave-one-lake-out spatial validation, and it gives a more nuanced land-cover map than the fixed threshold but still cannot on its own distinguish desilting or hyacinth from true encroachment without the added classes we built in.
